_about: Hand-picked artifacts tied to Bible passages; summaries and photos from Wikipedia (CC BY-SA). Built from scripts/build-relics.py.

relics.museum: Louvre, Paris
relics.x: The Mesha Stele, also known as the Moabite Stone, is a stele dated around 840 BCE containing a significant Canaanite inscription in the name of King Mesha of Moab. Mesha tells how Chemosh, the god of Moab, had been angry with his people and had allowed them to be subjugated to the Kingdom of Israel, but at length, Chem

relics.museum: Israel Museum, Jerusalem
relics.x: The Tel Dan Stele is a fragmentary stele with an Old Aramaic inscription written in the Phoenician script. It is generally dated to the 9th-century BCE, though some scholars have proposed later dates; it is one of the earliest, extra-biblical references to a Davidic dynasty. In 1993, it was discovered by Gila Cook, a m

relics.museum: British Museum, London
relics.x: The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III is a black limestone Neo-Assyrian sculpture with many scenes in bas-relief and inscriptions. It comes from Nimrud, in northern Iraq, and commemorates the deeds of King Shalmaneser III. It is on display at the British Museum in London, and several other museums have cast replicas.

relics.museum: British Museum / Oriental Institute
relics.x: Sennacherib's Annals are the annals of Sennacherib, emperor of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. They are found inscribed on several artifacts, and the final versions were found in three clay prisms inscribed with the same text: the Taylor Prism is in the British Museum, the ISAC or Chicago Prism in the Institute for the Study

relics.museum: British Museum, London
relics.x: The Lachish reliefs are a set of Assyrian palace reliefs narrating the story of the Assyrian victory over the kingdom of Judah during the siege of Lachish in 701 BC. Carved between 700 and 681 BC, as a decoration of the South-West Palace of Sennacherib in Nineveh, the relief is today in the British Museum in London, an

relics.museum: Istanbul Archaeology Museums
relics.x: The Siloam inscription, Silwan inscription or Shiloah inscription, known as KAI 189, is a Hebrew inscription found in the Siloam tunnel which brings water from the Gihon Spring to the Pool of Siloam, located in the City of David in East Jerusalem neighborhood of Silwan. The inscription records the construction of the t

relics.museum: British Museum, London
relics.x: The Cyrus Cylinder is an ancient clay cylinder, now broken into several pieces, on which is written an Achaemenid royal inscription in Akkadian cuneiform script in the name of the Persian king Cyrus the Great. It dates from the 6th century BC and was discovered in the ruins of the ancient Mesopotamian city of Babylon i

relics.museum: British Museum, London
relics.x: The Cylinders of Nabonidus refers to cuneiform inscriptions of king Nabonidus of Babylonia. These inscriptions were made on clay cylinders. They include the Nabonidus Cylinder from Sippar, and the Nabonidus Cylinders from Ur, four in number.

relics.t: Babylonian Chronicle of Nebuchadnezzar's siege of Jerusalem
relics.museum: British Museum, London
relics.x: The Babylonian Chronicles are a loosely defined series of about 45 tablets recording major events in Babylonian history.

relics.museum: Pergamon Museum, Berlin
relics.x: Jehoiachin's rations tablets date from the 6th century BC and describe the oil rations set aside for a royal captive identified as Jeconiah, king of Judah. Tablets from the royal archives of Nebuchadnezzar II, emperor of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, were unearthed in the ruins of Babylon that contain food rations paid to

relics.museum: Pergamon Museum, Berlin
relics.x: The Ishtar Gate was the eighth gate to the inner city wall of Babylon. It was constructed c. 569 BC by order of King Nebuchadnezzar II on the north side of the city. It was part of a grand walled processional way leading into the city.

relics.museum: Egyptian Museum, Cairo
relics.x: The Merneptah Stele, also known as the Israel Stele or the Victory Stele of Merneptah, is an inscription by Merneptah, a pharaoh in ancient Egypt who reigned from 1213 to 1203 BCE. Discovered by Flinders Petrie at Thebes in 1896, it is now housed at the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

relics.museum: Israel Museum, Jerusalem
relics.x: The Ketef Hinnom scrolls, also described as Ketef Hinnom amulets, are the oldest surviving texts currently known from the Hebrew Bible, dated to c. 600 BCE. The text, written in the Paleo-Hebrew script, has fragmentary phrases and words paralleling the Book of Numbers in the Hebrew Bible, and has been described as "one

relics.t: Flood tablet (Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet XI)
relics.museum: British Museum, London
relics.x:
The Gilgamesh flood myth is a partial narrative of the Gilgamesh Epic. It is one of three Mesopotamian flood myths alongside the one included in the Eridu Genesis, and an episode from the Atra-Hasis Epic. 
Many scholars believe that the Gilgamesh flood myth was added to Tablet XI in the "standard version" of the Gilgam

relics.museum: British Museum, London
relics.x: Enūma Eliš, meaning "When on High", is a Babylonian creation myth from the late 2nd millennium BCE and the only complete surviving account of ancient near eastern cosmology. It was recovered by English archaeologist Austen Henry Layard in 1849 in the ruined Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh. A form of the myth was fir

relics.museum: Louvre, Paris
relics.x: The Code of Hammurabi is a Babylonian legal text composed c. 1753 BC. It is the longest, best-organized, and best-preserved legal text from the ancient Near East. It is written in the Old Babylonian dialect of Akkadian, purportedly by Hammurabi, sixth king of the First Dynasty of Babylon. The primary copy of the text i

relics.museum: British Museum and others
relics.x: The Amarna letters are an archive, written on clay tablets, primarily consisting of diplomatic correspondence between the Egyptian administration and its representatives in Canaan and Amurru, or neighboring kingdom leaders, during the New Kingdom, spanning a period of no more than thirty years in the middle of the 14th

relics.museum: British Museum, London
relics.x: The Kurkh Monoliths are two Assyrian stelae of c. 852 BC and 879 BC that contain a description of the reigns of Ashurnasirpal II and his son Shalmaneser III. The Monoliths were discovered in 1861 by a British archaeologist John George Taylor, who was the British Consul-General stationed in the Ottoman Eyalet of Kurdist

relics.museum: Louvre, Paris
relics.x: Sargon II was the king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 722 BC to his death in battle in 705. Most likely the son of Tiglath-Pileser III, Sargon is generally believed to have become king after overthrowing Shalmaneser V, most likely his brother. He is typically considered the founder of a new dynastic line, the Sargonid

relics.museum: Karnak Temple, Luxor
relics.x: The Bubastite Portal is a gate is located in Karnak, within the Precinct of Amun-Re temple complex, between the temple of Ramesses III and the second pylon. It records the conquests and military campaigns c. 925 BC of Shoshenq I, of the Twenty-second Dynasty. Shoshenq has been identified with the biblical Shishaq, such

relics.museum: British Museum and Israel Museum
relics.x: The Lachish Letters are a series of letters written in carbon ink containing ancient Israelite inscriptions in Ancient Hebrew on clay ostraca. The letters were discovered at the excavations at Lachish.

relics.museum: Jerusalem
relics.x: The term Pool of Siloam refers to several rock-cut pools located southeast of the walls of the Old City of Jerusalem. The pools were fed by the waters of the Gihon Spring, carried there by the Siloam tunnel.

relics.museum: Jerusalem
relics.x: The Pool of Bethesda is referred to in John's Gospel in the Christian New Testament, in an account of Jesus healing a paralyzed man at a pool of water in Jerusalem, described as being near the Sheep Gate and surrounded by five covered colonnades or porticoes. It is also referred to as Bethzatha. It is now associated wi

relics.museum: Israel Museum, Jerusalem
relics.x: The Pilate stone is a damaged block of carved limestone, with dimensions 82 cm × 65 cm, which bears a partially intact inscription attributed to Pontius Pilate, a prefect of the Roman province of Judaea in the 1st century AD. It was discovered at the archaeological site of Caesarea Maritima in 1961.

relics.museum: Israel Museum, Jerusalem
relics.x: The Caiaphas ossuary is one of twelve ossuaries or bone boxes, discovered in a burial cave in south Jerusalem in December 1990, two of which featured the name "Caiaphas".

relics.museum: Yigal Allon Centre, Ginosar
relics.x: The Ancient Galilee Boat, also known as the Jesus Boat, is an ancient fishing boat from the 1st century AD, discovered in 1986 on the north-west shore of the Sea of Galilee in Israel. The remains of the boat, 27 feet long, 7.5 feet wide and with a maximum preserved height of 4.3 feet, first appeared during a drought, w

relics.museum: Istanbul Archaeology Museums
relics.x: The Temple Warning inscription, also known as the Temple Balustrade inscription or the Soreg inscription, is an inscription that hung along the balustrade outside the Sanctuary of the Second Temple in Jerusalem. Two of these tablets have been found. The inscription was a warning to pagan visitors to the temple not to p

relics.museum: Delphi Archaeological Museum
relics.x: The Delphi Inscription, or Gallio Inscription, is the name given to the collection of nine fragments of a letter written by the Roman emperor Claudius in 52 CE which was discovered early in the 20th century at the Temple of Apollo in Delphi, Greece.

relics.museum: Ancient Corinth
relics.x: Erastus of Corinth, also known as Erastus of Paneas, held the political office of steward, in Corinth, according to the Epistle to the Romans 16:23 of the New Testament. The office is defined as "the manager of household or of household affairs" or, in this context, "treasurer". The King James Version uses the translat

relics.t: Arch of Titus (spoils of the Temple)
relics.museum: Roman Forum, Rome
relics.x: The Arch of Titus is a 1st-century AD honorific arch, located on the Via Sacra, Rome, just to the south-east of the Roman Forum. It was constructed in c. 81 AD by Emperor Domitian shortly after the death of his older brother Titus to commemorate Titus's official deification or consecratio and the victory of Titus toget

relics.museum: Ephesus, Turkey
relics.x: Ephesus was an ancient Greek city on the coast of Ionia, in present-day Selçuk in İzmir Province, Turkey. It was built in the 10th century BC on the site of Apasa, a city-state that was also the capital of Arzawa, by Attic and Ionian Greek colonists. During the Classical Greek era, it was one of twelve cities that were

relics.museum: Capernaum, Galilee
relics.x: Capernaum was a fishing village established during the time of the Hasmoneans in Israel, located on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee. It had a population of about 1,500 in the 1st century AD. Archaeological excavations have revealed two ancient synagogues built successively at the same spot. A house progressive

relics.museum: Shrine of the Book, Israel Museum
relics.x: The Isaiah Scroll, designated 1QIsaa and also known as the Great Isaiah Scroll, is one of the seven Dead Sea Scrolls that were first discovered by Bedouin shepherds in 1947 from Qumran Cave 1. The scroll is written in Hebrew and contains the entire Book of Isaiah from beginning to end, apart from a few small damaged po

relics.museum: Cambridge University Library
relics.x: The Nash Papyrus is a collection of four papyrus fragments acquired in Egypt in 1902, inscribed with a Hebrew text which mainly contains the Ten Commandments and the first part of the Shema Yisrael prayer, in a form that differs substantially from the later, canonical Masoretic Text and is in parts more similar to the

relics.museum: John Rylands Library, Manchester
relics.x: The Rylands Library Papyrus P52, also known as the St John's fragment and with an accession reference of Papyrus Rylands Greek 457, is a fragment from a papyrus codex, measuring 3.5 by 2.5 inches at its widest, and conserved with the Rylands Papyri at the John Rylands University Library Manchester, UK. The front (recto

relics.museum: British Library, London
relics.x: The Codex Sinaiticus, also called the Sinai Bible, is a fourth-century Christian manuscript of a Greek Bible, containing the majority of the Greek Old Testament, including the deuterocanonical books, and the Greek New Testament, with both the Epistle of Barnabas and the Shepherd of Hermas included. It is designated by

relics.museum: Schøyen Collection
relics.x: Etemenanki was a Babylonian ziggurat dedicated to the Mesopotamian god Marduk. It is now in ruins, which are located about 90 kilometres (56 mi) south of Baghdad. Some scholars have proposed Etemenanki as the ziggurat that may have influenced the biblical account of the Tower of Babel.

relics.t: Nineveh, the city Jonah preached to
relics.museum: Mosul, Iraq (reliefs in the British Museum)
relics.x: Nineveh was an ancient Near Eastern city of Upper Mesopotamia, located in the modern-day city of Mosul in northern Iraq. It is located on the eastern bank of the Tigris River and was the capital and largest city of the Neo-Assyrian Empire, and potentially the wealthiest city in the ancient world. Today, it is a common

relics.museum: Ram's-horn shofars in Jewish museum collections; ancient forms shown on synagogue mosaics
relics.x: The shofar is a hollowed ram's horn, the same instrument the priests blew as they circled Jericho.

relics.museum: Grand Egyptian Museum, Giza (formerly Egyptian Museum, Cairo)
relics.x: These silver and bronze trumpets from about 1320 BC show the long straight metal trumpet of the kind Moses was told to hammer out of silver.

relics.museum: British Museum, London; Penn Museum, Philadelphia; Iraq Museum, Baghdad
relics.x: These lyres from the royal tombs of Ur show the wooden frame and strings of the instrument the Bible calls a kinnor, the lyre David played.

relics.museum: Depicted on Bar Kokhba coins and Iron Age seals and ivories
relics.x: Ancient images of the kinnor show a small hand-held lyre with a yoke and strings, the instrument David played for Saul.

relics.museum: Known from ancient Near Eastern reliefs and depictions
relics.x: The nevel was a larger stringed instrument than the kinnor, and ancient images show the kind of harp named alongside the lyre in the Psalms.

relics.museum: Egyptian examples in the British Museum, Louvre and Metropolitan Museum of Art
relics.x: Ancient sistrums are metal rattles on a handle, the instrument many translations see in the noise of celebration as David brought up the ark.

relics.museum: Bronze examples excavated across the Near East and Mediterranean
relics.x: Small bronze cymbals from antiquity show the clashing plates the Levite musicians struck and Paul had in mind for a noisy cymbal.

relics.museum: Many Iron Age clay figurines of women holding frame drums, e.g. Israel Museum
relics.x: Clay figurines from Iron Age Israel show women holding a round frame drum, the toph Miriam played after the Red Sea crossing.

relics.museum: Greek and Roman examples in the British Museum and Louvre
relics.x: The aulos was the double reed pipe of the Greek and Roman world, the instrument of the flute players at the house of Jairus.

relics.museum: Ancient sling remains and depictions in many collections
relics.x: A shepherd's sling was a pouch on two cords, the weapon David used to bring down Goliath.

relics.museum: Bronze scales excavated at Near Eastern sites
relics.x: Bronze scale armour was made of overlapping metal plates, the kind of coat of mail Goliath wore.

relics.museum: Bronze examples in Greek and Mediterranean collections
relics.x: Ancient bronze greaves are shin guards, the exact piece of armour the text says Goliath wore on his legs.

relics.museum: Roman examples in many museums, including the Sword of Tiberius, British Museum, London
relics.x: The gladius was the Roman legionary's short sword, the blade Paul calls the sword of the Spirit.

relics.museum: Excavated examples from Corbridge and Kalkriese
relics.x: The banded iron body armour of the Roman legionary shows the breastplate Paul tells believers to put on.

relics.museum: Yale University Art Gallery (the Dura-Europos scutum)
relics.x: The Roman scutum was a large curved door-shaped shield, the thureos Paul names as the shield of faith.

relics.museum: Roman examples in many museums
relics.x: Roman legionary helmets show the helmet of salvation Paul pictured on the soldier guarding him.

relics.museum: Excavated examples from Vindolanda and other Roman forts
relics.x: Roman military boots were hobnailed sandals built for marching, the footwear behind Paul's feet fitted with the gospel of peace.

relics.museum: Excavated fittings in many Roman collections
relics.x: The Roman soldier's belt held his gear and marked his rank, the belt Paul calls the belt of truth.

relics.museum: Shown on Assyrian palace reliefs in the British Museum
relics.x: Assyrian reliefs show wheeled battering rams against city walls, the siege engine Ezekiel was told to set against his model of Jerusalem.

relics.museum: Shown on Assyrian palace reliefs; Greek and Roman examples reconstructed
relics.x: Ancient siege engines were machines for attacking or defending walls, the kind Uzziah built to shoot arrows and great stones.

relics.museum: Israel Museum, Jerusalem; British Museum, London
relics.x: The silver shekel of Tyre was the coin required for the temple tax and the likeliest coin in the thirty pieces of silver paid to Judas.

relics.museum: British Museum, London, and many coin collections
relics.x: The silver denarius of Tiberius carries the emperor's face and title, the image and inscription Jesus asked about.

relics.museum: Roman coin collections worldwide
relics.x: The denarius was a silver coin worth a labourer's day wage, the pay in the parable of the vineyard workers.

relics.museum: Israel Museum, Jerusalem, and many coin collections
relics.x: The tiny bronze lepton, often struck by Alexander Jannaeus, is the smallest coin in circulation and the one the widow gave.

relics.museum: Roman coin collections worldwide
relics.x: The quadrans was the smallest Roman bronze coin, the one Mark uses to explain the value of the widow's two lepta.

relics.museum: Roman coin collections worldwide
relics.x: The bronze as, called assarion in Greek, is the small coin that bought two sparrows.

relics.museum: Greek coin collections worldwide
relics.x: The silver drachma was a day's wage coin of the Greek world, the coin the woman swept the house to find.

relics.museum: British Museum, London
relics.x: The gold daric of the Persian kings is the coin counted in the gifts for rebuilding the temple.

relics.museum: British Museum, London; Israel Museum, Jerusalem
relics.x: Rome struck these coins showing a mourning woman under a palm to celebrate the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 that Jesus foretold.

relics.museum: Excavated widely in Judea; Israel Museum, Jerusalem
relics.x: The small clay oil lamp of the period held only a little oil, which is why the wise virgins carried extra in flasks.

relics.museum: Excavated examples from Vindolanda, Pompeii and Egypt
relics.x: A wooden tablet coated with wax was the everyday notepad of the Roman world, what Zechariah asked for to write his son's name.

relics.museum: Dead Sea Scrolls at the Shrine of the Book, Israel Museum
relics.x: Ancient scrolls were long sheets of leather or papyrus rolled up, the kind Baruch wrote and Jesus unrolled in the synagogue.

relics.museum: Papyrus documents in the British Library, Chester Beatty and many collections
relics.x: Papyrus sheets were the paper of the ancient world, the paper John says he would rather not use.

relics.museum: Ancient parchment manuscripts in many collections
relics.x: Parchment was prepared animal skin for writing, the parchments Paul asked Timothy to bring.

relics.museum: Egyptian examples in the British Museum and Metropolitan Museum of Art
relics.x: Ancient scribes carried a palette with ink wells and reed pens, the writing case on the hip of the man in linen in Ezekiel's vision.

relics.museum: British Museum, Louvre and many Near Eastern collections
relics.x: A cylinder seal rolled across wet clay leaves its picture behind, the image behind clay under the seal in Job.

relics.museum: Hundreds of Judean bullae in the Israel Museum and other collections
relics.x: Clay bullae pressed with a seal closed rolled documents, the way Jeremiah's land deed was sealed.

relics.museum: Israel Museum, Jerusalem, and many excavated jar handles
relics.x: Jar handles stamped 'belonging to the king' come from Hezekiah's reign and show the royal storehouses he filled.

relics.museum: Brooklyn Museum; Egyptian Museum of Berlin
relics.x: These Jewish letters from Persian Egypt name Sanballat governor of Samaria and Johanan the high priest, men Nehemiah also names.

relics.museum: British Library, Louvre, Berlin and other collections
relics.x: These papyrus spell books show the kind of magic books the Ephesians burned.

relics.museum: Small household figurines excavated at Near Eastern sites
relics.x: Teraphim were household god images small enough for Rachel to hide in a camel saddle.

relics.museum: Israel Museum, Jerusalem
relics.x: Hundreds of these clay figurines from Judah are often linked to the goddess worship Josiah purged and Jeremiah condemned.

relics.museum: Louvre, Paris
relics.x: This stele from Ugarit shows Baal as a storm god raising a club and a lightning spear, the god Elijah confronted on Carmel.

relics.museum: Excavated at Tel Arad and other sites; Israel Museum, Jerusalem
relics.x: A massebah is an upright standing stone, like the pillar Jacob set up at Bethel.

relics.museum: Grand Egyptian Museum, Giza (formerly Egyptian Museum, Cairo)
relics.x: This gilded chest from Tutankhamun's tomb rides on carrying poles, like the ark carried by the priests.

relics.museum: British Museum, Louvre and Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, Chicago
relics.x: Assyrian guardian figures combine a man's face, a bull's body, a lion's strength and eagle's wings, the same mix Ezekiel saw in the living creatures.

relics.museum: British Museum, London
relics.x: Statues of the Babylonian god Nabu show the idol Isaiah calls Nebo, carried off on beasts of burden.

relics.museum: Shown on Babylonian cylinder seals and boundary stones
relics.x: Babylonian images of Marduk show the chief god the prophets call Bel and Merodach.

relics.museum: Excavated at the Magdala synagogue
relics.x: This carved stone from a first-century synagogue shows a seven-branched lampstand, probably cut by someone who had seen the temple menorah.

relics.museum: British Museum, London; Penn Museum, Philadelphia
relics.x: Excavators named this gold goat statue from Ur after Genesis 22:13 because it shows a horned animal caught in a bush.

relics.museum: Tefillin cases and slips found in the Qumran caves
relics.x: Tefillin found at Qumran are tiny leather boxes holding Scripture slips, the phylacteries Jesus said some made broad for show.

relics.museum: Mezuzah texts found at Qumran
relics.x: A mezuzah is a small Scripture case fixed to a doorpost, the practice taken from writing the words on the doorposts.

relics.museum: Shown on ancient textiles and depictions
relics.x: Tzitzit are the knotted tassels on a garment's corners, the fringe the bleeding woman touched.

relics.museum: Rockefeller Museum, Jerusalem
relics.x: This first-century inscription records a Jerusalem synagogue built for reading the law and housing visitors, the kind Diaspora Jews attended in Acts 6.

relics.museum: Excavated at many Israelite and Near Eastern sites
relics.x: A hand mill of two stones ground grain at home, the mill two women grind at in Matthew 24:41.

relics.museum: Roman donkey mills preserved at Pompeii and Capernaum
relics.x: Large Roman millstones turned by a donkey are the mylos onikos Jesus spoke of hanging around the neck.

relics.museum: Traditional examples in agricultural museums
relics.x: A threshing sledge was a heavy board studded with sharp stones or iron dragged over grain, the tool Isaiah and Amos describe.

relics.museum: Ancient examples and depictions in many collections
relics.x: The simple scratch plough pulled by oxen is the plough Elisha drove and Jesus said not to look back from.

relics.museum: Rock-cut winepresses excavated across Israel
relics.x: Excavated winepresses are rock-cut treading floors draining into a vat, the press dug in the vineyard of Isaiah 5 and Matthew 21.

relics.museum: Excavated at Tel Miqne-Ekron, Capernaum and many sites
relics.x: Ancient olive presses crushed and squeezed olives for oil, and Gethsemane means oil press.

relics.museum: Ancient stone wheel bearings excavated at Hazor, Lachish and elsewhere
relics.x: The potter's wheel of stone turned by hand or foot is what Jeremiah watched the potter working at.

relics.museum: Ancient Egyptian and Roman examples in many collections
relics.x: A plumb line is a weight on a cord to test a wall for true, the line the Lord held against Israel in Amos 7.

relics.museum: Excavated at nearly every Iron Age site in Israel
relics.x: Spindle whorls are the weights on a hand spindle, the tool of the woman in Proverbs 31 spinning thread.

relics.museum: Loom weights excavated at many Iron Age sites
relics.x: Upright looms with a heavy wooden beam explain why Goliath's spear shaft was compared to a weaver's beam.

relics.museum: Excavated clay ovens at Israelite sites
relics.x: The clay taboon was a small domed household oven, the oven of the grain offering and of Hosea's image.

relics.museum: Stone examples excavated across the Near East
relics.x: A stone mortar and pestle crushed grain and spices, the way Israel prepared manna.

relics.museum: Stone mangers excavated at Megiddo and other sites
relics.x: Ancient feeding troughs were often carved from stone, the manger where Mary laid Jesus.

relics.museum: Traditional skins and ancient depictions
relics.x: Whole goatskins sewn up to carry wine stretched and cracked with age, which is why new wine needs new skins.

relics.museum: Examples in the British Museum, Louvre and Metropolitan Museum of Art
relics.x: An alabastron was a small narrow-necked flask for perfume, the alabaster jar broken over Jesus' head.

relics.museum: Egyptian and Levantine kohl tubes in many collections
relics.x: Kohl was black eye paint kept in small tubes, what Jezebel put on before Jehu arrived.

relics.museum: Murex shell heaps excavated at Tyre and Sidon
relics.x: Purple dye from murex sea snails was costly, the trade of Lydia and the robe of the rich man.

relics.museum: Egyptian mummies in the British Museum, Cairo and many collections
relics.x: Egyptian mummies show the embalming that took forty days for Jacob and placed Joseph in a coffin in Egypt.

relics.museum: Excavated at Givat HaMivtar, Jerusalem; replica in the Israel Museum
relics.x: The heel bone of a crucified man named Yehohanan still has the iron nail through it, physical evidence of Roman crucifixion in Jerusalem.

relics.museum: Palatine Museum, Rome
relics.x: This Roman wall scratching mocks a Christian worshipping a crucified figure with a donkey's head, the foolishness of the cross Paul names.

relics.museum: Known from ancient sources and later examples
relics.x: Stocks clamped a prisoner's feet in a wooden frame, how Paul and Silas were held at Philippi.

relics.museum: Excavated in Jerusalem
relics.x: This first-century Jerusalem tomb still has its round blocking stone, the kind rolled across the entrance of Jesus' tomb.

relics.museum: Kyrenia Castle Shipwreck Museum, Cyprus
relics.x: This small Greek merchant ship from about 300 BC shows the kind of coastal trading vessel Jonah boarded at Joppa.

relics.museum: Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology, Turkey
relics.x: This Late Bronze Age wreck carried copper, tin, glass, ivory and spices, the mixed cargo of the trade Ezekiel lists for Tyre.

relics.museum: Grand Egyptian Museum, Giza (formerly Egyptian Museum, Cairo)
relics.x: These light two-wheeled Egyptian chariots show the vehicle Pharaoh's army drove into the sea.

relics.museum: Theban tomb TT100, Luxor
relics.x: Paintings in this tomb show foreign labourers making mud bricks under taskmasters, the work Israel did in Egypt.

relics.museum: Excavated at Tell el-Muqayyar, Iraq
relics.x: This stepped brick temple tower from Abram's city shows the kind of tower the builders of Babel set out to make.

relics.museum: Jordan Archaeological Museum, Amman
relics.x: This plaster text names Balaam son of Beor as a seer of the gods, the same prophet hired by Balak.

relics.museum: Excavated at Persepolis and Susa
relics.x: The columned audience halls of the Persian kings show the setting of the king's feast in Esther 1.

relics.museum: British Museum, London
relics.x: Gold cups and ornaments from the Persian empire show the kind of golden vessels served at Ahasuerus's banquet.

relics.museum: British Museum, London
relics.x: In this stone text Nebuchadnezzar boasts of building Babylon, the same boast he makes in Daniel 4.

relics.museum: British Museum, London
relics.x: This Babylonian omen tablet records Venus sightings to predict the future, the star-gazing Isaiah mocked.

relics.museum: Babylonian clay liver models, British Museum, London; Etruscan bronze Liver of Piacenza, Piacenza
relics.x: Ancient liver models, Babylonian clay ones and the later Etruscan bronze liver of Piacenza, were used to read omens, the method the king of Babylon used at the crossroads.

relics.museum: Vatican Museums, Rome
relics.x: This statue shows Augustus as the emperor whose decree sent Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem.

relics.museum: Pergamon Museum, Berlin
relics.x: This stele from Sam'al shows Esarhaddon holding captives by cords fixed to rings through their lips, the treatment the prophets meant by a hook in the nose.

relics.museum: Excavated at Beni Hasan, Egypt
relics.x: A wall painting in his tomb shows a Semitic clan with donkeys and colourful clothes arriving in Egypt, like the patriarchs' journeys.
